readingInstruction: Read Nahum 1:1-3:19. Nahum is a short prophecy of about fifty verses against Nineveh, the Assyrian capital. This is the same city that repented under Jonah. Read it with Jonah in mind, and ask what has changed.
settingTheScene: Nahum prophesied in the seventh century BC, sometime after the fall of Thebes in 663 BC and before the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC. A hundred and fifty years earlier, Nineveh had repented at Jonah’s preaching. In the generations since, the city returned to violence and cruelty and became the capital of the empire that destroyed Samaria and tormented Judah. Nahum’s message is that God’s patience, though long, has an end.
observation: “The LORD is a jealous and avenging God; the LORD is avenging and wrathful” (1:2).
“The LORD is slow to anger and great in power, and the LORD will by no means clear the guilty” (1:3).
“The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him” (1:7).
“Behold, on the mountains, the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace!” (1:15).
“Woe to the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder” (3:1).
“Behold, I am against you, declares the LORD of hosts” (3:5).
“There is no easing your hurt; your wound is grievous” (3:19).
“For upon whom has not come your unceasing evil?” (3:19).
interpretation:
The book opens with a majestic hymn about God’s character, drawing on Exodus 34:6-7. But Nahum emphasizes a different side. He quotes “slow to anger” and then, “will by no means clear the guilty.” God’s patience is not indifference. A holy God must respond to evil. The imagery is of a storm: mountains quake, hills melt, the earth heaves. Who can stand before his indignation? And in the middle, a note of gentle comfort: “The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him.” To the same God, the wicked experience a fire, and the faithful a refuge. Everything depends on which side of him we stand.

The word to Judah in 1:12-15 is a comfort: “Though I have afflicted you, I will afflict you no more.” The yoke of Assyria will be broken. And the herald appears on the mountains with good news. Isaiah 52:7 uses the same image, which Paul applies to the preaching of the gospel in Romans 10:15.

Chapters 2 and 3 describe the fall of Nineveh with vivid military imagery: shields red, chariots flashing, the river gates opening, the palace dissolving. In 612 BC, the city fell when the Tigris flooded and broke part of the wall, and the Babylonians and Medes entered. The prophet describes the city as a den of lions that fed on prey and filled its caves with plunder. “Behold, I am against you.” Her sins are violence, deceit, plunder, and sorceries. She will be exposed, shamed, and no one will mourn.

The book ends with a rhetorical question that reminds us of Jonah: “For upon whom has not come your unceasing evil?” The contrast with the book of Jonah is a lesson. In Jonah’s day, the city repented and was spared. In Nahum’s day, the city had returned to evil and was not spared. God’s mercy is real, and God’s justice is real. Both come from the same character. No generation can live on the repentance of a previous one.
connection: Romans 11:22 says, “Note then the kindness and the severity of God.” Romans 10:15 applies Nahum 1:15 to those who bring the gospel. Jesus’ comparison in Matthew 12:41 says the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment. 2 Peter 3:9 says the Lord is patient, not wishing that any should perish, and verse 10 says the day of the Lord will come. Hebrews 12:29 says our God is a consuming fire. Psalm 34:8 invites us to taste and see that the LORD is good.
application:
Take refuge in the LORD, who is good, and thank him that you are known by him.

Ask whether you are presuming on God’s patience in any area.

Pray for a violent or oppressive regime in the world today, that justice would come and the oppressed would be freed.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he is slow to anger and great in power.
Thank him that he is a stronghold and knows those who take refuge in him.
Pray for those who suffer under cruelty.
